records.title: The Arkansas Traveler
records.description:
*The Arkansas Traveler* is the oldest thing on any of these records — a fiddle tune and a stage routine, both of them older than the phonograph. In its standard form a traveller stops at a squatter's cabin and asks a string of reasonable questions; the squatter, sawing away at the same eight bars, answers every one of them with a joke, and only when the stranger takes the fiddle and plays the turn of the tune does he get supper and a bed. The dialogue was in print by the 1850s and was a staple of variety houses long before anybody thought of recording it.

Len Spencer's version of the sketch was one of the standard talking-machine records of the period, and Indestructible put it into the four-minute series at 3020, near the very beginning of that series. The extra two minutes are the point: at four minutes the whole exchange fits, where the two-minute cylinder had to cut the routine to a fragment. Records like this — a talking piece with a fiddle behind it — were exactly the sort of thing that sold a four-minute machine to somebody who already owned a two-minute one.

Spencer was the house monologuist of the American record business, and dialect sketches of this kind made up a good share of the catalogues of every company. This one has the additional interest of being early enough to sit right at the start of Indestructible's four-minute run, when the Albany company was selling through Columbia and was, briefly, the most visible competitor Edison had in the cylinder trade.

records.title: Goodnight, Little Girl, Goodnight
records.description:
A parlour goodnight song of the sentimental kind that Henry Burr could sell better than anyone else in the business. The words are a lover's leave-taking at the door, and the tune is built for the long-breathed, slightly nasal tenor line that carried well through an acoustic horn — which is precisely why it turns up over and over in cylinder catalogues on both sides of the two-minute/ four-minute divide.

Indestructible issued the song twice under two different numbers: at 1186 in the two-minute series and here at 3052 in the four-minute series. That pairing is worth noticing, because it shows how the Albany company worked. It did not simply retire the old series when the four-minute records arrived in 1909; it ran the two side by side for years, remaking the reliable sellers at the longer length and leaving the short version in the catalogue for the enormous installed base of two-minute machines.

For an Amberola owner this is one of the more useful sorts of Indestructible to look for: a straightforward vocal with light accompaniment, recorded loud, on a material that has usually come through the last century better than the wax Amberol of the same song would have.

records.title: La Gitana
records.description:
*La Gitana* — "the gypsy girl" — is one of the Spanish-flavoured intermezzos that every band in America played in the years either side of 1910, a genre that ran from Bizet imitations to the Moorish serenades of the Sousa repertoire. Pieces of this kind were staples of the cylinder catalogues because a band recorded well: brass and reeds put enough energy into the horn to cut a strong groove, where a string orchestra tended to disappear.

The Indestructible copy is credited in the one listing that documents it simply to a band, with no further identification. That is normal for the label. Indestructible used studio groups billed as the Indestructible Band or, on some issues, as nothing more specific than "Band", and the personnel behind those names is largely unrecorded. Rather than attach a plausible bandmaster's name to it, this entry leaves the performer blank.

Band selections are also the cylinders most worth hearing on the celluloid records specifically. The Indestructible surface is harder and brighter than wax, which flatters loud ensemble playing and can make a four-minute band record noticeably more present than the equivalent Amberol.

records.title: Honey, I Will Long for You
records.description:
A duet for two of the most familiar voices on American records: Frank C. Stanley, the bass and banjoist whose real name was William Stanley Grinsted, and Henry Burr, the tenor who by 1910 was recording for practically everybody. The Stanley–Burr partnership was one of the standard duet teams of the decade, and its records — close-harmony sentimental songs, usually with a small orchestra — were made for every label that would have them.

The pairing also dates this issue within fairly narrow limits. Stanley died at the end of 1910, so any Stanley–Burr record must have been made before that, and the number sits in the block Indestructible was issuing while its output was being distributed nationally by the Columbia Phonograph Company. A four-minute celluloid of this vintage would have been sold in both an Albany box and a Columbia one, the record inside being identical.

The song itself has not left much of a trace outside the cylinder catalogues, which is a common fate for the second-rank popular songs of the period: they were written for the trade, recorded within weeks, and dropped when the next one came along. The cylinder is often the only surviving evidence that anybody performed them at all.

records.title: When You and I Were Young, Maggie
records.description:
George W. Johnson wrote the poem in 1864 for Maggie Clark, a young woman he was courting near Hamilton, Ontario; she died not long after they married. James Austin Butterfield set it to music in 1866, and the song became one of the permanent fixtures of the English-language parlour repertoire — a backward look at a mill, a hill and a creek that are still there while the singer and Maggie are not. Every recording company of the acoustic era carried a version, Edison included.

Indestructible's four-minute copy is credited to the baritone Frank Coombs, a singer who appears regularly on the independent labels and about whom very little has been written. The four-minute length suits the song: at two minutes the verses had to be cut, while a four-minute cylinder can carry the whole thing at a walking tempo, which is how it was meant to go.

Coombs's version belongs to the later stretch of the four-minute run, and it is exactly the kind of record the Albany company built its catalogue on. Indestructible signed no famous artists. It hired the reliable freelance singers of the New York studios, recorded the songs everybody already knew, and sold the result on the claim that its record would still play when a wax one had worn out.

records.title: Home Sweet Home
records.description:
*Home! Sweet Home!* began life in 1823 as an air in the opera *Clari, or the Maid of Milan* — words by the American playwright John Howard Payne, music by the English composer Sir Henry Bishop — and within a generation it had escaped the theatre entirely. By the 1860s it was the song soldiers on both sides of the American Civil War were said to have sung across the lines at each other; by the 1900s it was the piece a talking machine dealer put on to close a sale.

The copy documented at 3213 carries no artist credit in the listing that records it, and no performer has been supplied here. This is a real and common gap in the Indestructible literature: the surviving boxes and lids often name the singer, but a bare cylinder rarely does, and the printed numerical lists for the label are patchy in a way the Edison lists are not.

The song's ubiquity is itself the historical point. Every cylinder maker had a *Home Sweet Home*, and having one was almost a condition of being taken seriously as a record company. For Indestructible, in the middle of a decade-long argument with Edison about who was entitled to make moulded celluloid cylinders at all, carrying the standard repertoire was part of the claim to be a full competitor rather than a novelty.

records.title: Baby Rose
records.description:
Arthur Collins and Byron G. Harlan were the most successful duet team in American records, a baritone and a tenor who between them covered comic songs, rustic sketches, minstrel material and the ragtime hits of the day. Their names on a cylinder box were a selling point in themselves, and every label that could get them — Edison, Columbia, Victor, and the independents alike — used them heavily.

That they appear on four-minute Indestructible 3228 is a good illustration of how the independent cylinder trade actually worked. The Albany company had no exclusive artists. It booked the same freelance singers who were recording for Edison the same week, in the same few New York studios, which is why the Indestructible catalogue reads like a shadow of the Edison one. What Indestructible sold was not different performances but a different material: a celluloid record advertised as unbreakable and unwearable, against Edison's wax.

Collins and Harlan records also carry a good deal of the era's minstrel-derived material, and modern listeners should expect the racial caricature that went with it. It is part of why these cylinders are studied as documents as much as they are collected as music.

records.title: Oh! You Beautiful Doll
records.description:
A. Seymour Brown and Nat D. Ayer published *Oh! You Beautiful Doll* in 1911, and it went off like a rocket: a ragtime love song with a verse nobody remembers and a chorus everybody does. It was one of the defining hits of the last pre-war years and was recorded by essentially every company then making records, in vocal, band and dance versions.

Indestructible's four-minute issue of it at 3253 sits squarely inside the period when the Albany company's records were also being sold in Columbia boxes, which means a collector may find the same performance under two different brand names. The performer on this number is not established here, and no name has been attached to it. That is a deliberate gap: the song was recorded so widely that guessing at a plausible singer would be very easy and very likely wrong.

Songs like this are also the reason the four-minute celluloids matter musically. A hit of 1911 got its fullest cylinder treatment at four minutes — chorus repeats, an instrumental break, sometimes a patter verse — where the two-minute record had to sprint. On an Amberola, this is the format the machine was built for.

records.title: It's a Long Lane That Has No Turning
records.description:
A proverb song — the title is the old saying that no run of bad luck lasts forever — sung as a duet by the contralto Helen Clark and the tenor Walter Van Brunt. The two were Indestructible's standing duet team in the four-minute series, and they appear together in an unbroken little run of numbers in the 3250s to 3300s that reads like a snapshot of what was selling in the sheet-music shops of 1911 and 1912.

Van Brunt was still in his early twenties when these were made, at the start of a long career that would later continue under the name Walter Scanlan. Helen Clark is the more shadowy of the two; she recorded prolifically as a duet partner and hardly at all as a soloist, and the standard reference works have little to say about her beyond her repertoire.

The record is a good example of what the four-minute celluloid was for. A duet with an orchestra needs room — two verses, two choruses, an instrumental turn — and the extra length was Indestructible's answer to Edison's Amberol. The difference was that where Edison's four-minute record was wax with 200 threads to the inch and wore quickly, the Indestructible was celluloid and, in the company's advertising, would outlast the machine.

records.title: Goodbye Rose
records.description:
One of the parting-song ballads that Henry Burr recorded by the dozen — a farewell to a girl, a verse, a chorus written to be sung by a tenor at the top of his comfortable range, and an orchestra that stays out of the way. Burr's records of this kind were the commercial backbone of half the catalogues in the business, and Indestructible leaned on them as heavily as anyone.

The number places it in the earlier part of the four-minute run, in the years when the Albany company's cylinders were reaching dealers through Columbia. Columbia had given up making its own cylinders in favour of selling Indestructible's, an arrangement that lasted from 1908 until 1912 and briefly made these celluloid records the most widely distributed cylinders in America after Edison's.

When the Columbia agreement ended, Indestructible went back to selling under its own name and through Sears, whose Oxford brand carried the same records again under a third label. The company kept going until 1922, longer than any other American cylinder maker except Edison — which is why an Indestructible box turns up in three different liveries with the same number inside.

records.title: There's a Girl in Havana
records.description:
*There's a Girl in Havana* came out of the 1911 New York musical stage and belongs to the brief craze for Cuban and Latin-flavoured numbers that ran through American popular song either side of 1910. The rhythm is a mild habanera, the sentiment is a sailor's, and the tune was current exactly long enough to be recorded by everybody and then forgotten.

On Indestructible it is a Helen Clark and Walter Van Brunt duet, part of the same run of four-minute numbers in the 3250s and 3260s that the pair carried between them. Dating the issue from the song's publication puts it in 1911 or 1912, which is to say in the last months of Columbia's distribution agreement — the period in which the identical cylinder could reach a customer in a Columbia box, an Indestructible box, or an Oxford box from Sears, Roebuck.

For collectors the number is a useful marker. Anything in this stretch of the four-minute series is Columbia-era material, and a four-minute Indestructible found in a Columbia carton almost certainly carries a number from this part of the list.

records.title: On Moonlight Bay
records.description:
Percy Wenrich's melody and Edward Madden's words were published in 1912 and became one of the permanent barbershop standards — "we were sailing along, on Moonlight Bay" — a song whose afterlife in film and on television has long outrun any memory of who wrote it. In 1912 it was simply the hit of the season, and every record company in America made a version within weeks of the sheet music.

The Indestructible is a duet by Helen Clark and Walter Van Brunt, the label's regular four-minute pairing. This is one of the very few entries in this file that two independent sources agree on: the Deakins index lists the title and number under Clark and Van Brunt, and the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive holds a copy of Indestructible 3264 catalogued to the same two singers. Edison also issued the song on cylinder, as did the disc companies, so a collector can put several 1912 readings of it side by side.

It also sits at a hinge in the celluloid story. In 1912, the year of this record, Edison finally brought out the Blue Amberol — a celluloid cylinder of his own, with a plaster core — and Columbia walked away from its agreement to distribute Indestructible's. The independent that had spent five years arguing that celluloid was the future was proved right and undercut in the same season.

records.title: Love Never Dies
records.description:
Another of the Helen Clark and Walter Van Brunt four-minute duets, and one of the many songs of the period whose title outlived its music. Nothing has been established here about its authorship, and rather than attach a composer on the strength of a similar title, this entry says so plainly.

The value of an entry like this is as a piece of the numerical list. The surviving documentation for Indestructible is nothing like the month-by-month record that exists for Edison: there is no equivalent of the *Edison Phonograph Monthly* supplements, the company's own catalogues survive patchily, and modern knowledge of the series rests largely on two compilations — Duane Deakins's index of the 1950s and 60s and Major H. H. Annand's listing of 1970 — supplemented by whatever collectors have in hand.

That is the honest situation for most of the label. A number, a title and a pair of singers is often the whole of what can be said, and filling the rest of the page with invention would make the catalogue less useful, not more.

records.title: I'd Love to Live in Loveland
records.description:
W. R. Williams — the pen name of the Chicago publisher Will Rossiter — wrote *I'd Love to Live in Loveland with a Girl Like You* in 1910, and it became one of those songs that sold steadily for years without ever quite being fashionable. It is a waltz-time daydream about a place that does not exist, and its chorus was still being sung in barbershop arrangements decades later.

Henry Burr's four-minute Indestructible sits in the middle of the label's Columbia years. The company's whole proposition was on the box: a record that could be dropped, that would not shave or crumble, and that a dealer could demonstrate by throwing it on the floor. The claim was largely true. The reason so many Indestructibles survive in playable condition today, while contemporary wax Amberols are so often mouldy or worn to a whisper, is that the celluloid really was the better material.

What Indestructible could not survive was the litigation and the market. Edison pressed his patent position hard against every maker of moulded celluloid cylinders, and when he brought out his own celluloid record in 1912 the independents' technical advantage evaporated. Indestructible outlasted the rest of them by a decade, but it was selling into a shrinking cylinder trade the whole time.

records.title: You Made Me Love You
records.subtitle: I Didn't Want to Do It
records.description:
James V. Monaco's music and Joseph McCarthy's words were published in 1913 with the parenthetical subtitle *(I Didn't Want to Do It)*, and the song became one of the biggest of the pre-war years — later inseparable from Al Jolson, and later still from Judy Garland's 1937 letter to Clark Gable. The 1913 recordings, this one among them, catch it before any of that, as a straight popular song with a syncopated lilt.

Indestructible put it in the four-minute series as a Helen Clark and Walter Van Brunt duet. By 1913 the Columbia agreement was over, Edison's Blue Amberol was on sale, and the Albany company was back to selling under its own name and through the Sears Oxford brand. That it was still issuing the season's biggest hits shows how far from finished it was: production continued until 1922, when the Albany plant burned.

For a collector, four-minute numbers in the 3300s are the ones to look for in Indestructible-branded boxes rather than Columbia ones, and they are late enough that the recording quality is at the label's best.

records.title: The Holy City
records.description:
Stephen Adams — the stage name of the singer Michael Maybrick — set Frederic Weatherly's words in 1892, and *The Holy City* became the best-selling sacred ballad in the English language: Jerusalem seen three times, first in a dream, then in ruin, then in glory, with a chorus that climbs each time. It was the piece every ballad singer of the era had in his throat, and its recording history runs from the brown-wax cylinders of the 1890s to the electrical era.

Henry Burr's four-minute Indestructible is one of two versions of the song in the label's list; the other is at 676 in the two-minute series, made years earlier. Sacred and semi-sacred songs were a large and often overlooked part of the cylinder business — Sunday material for a machine bought for Saturday — and they held their place in the catalogues long after the popular songs around them had been withdrawn.

At four minutes the song can be taken at its proper unhurried pace and still fit, which was not true of a two-minute cylinder. This is the format the piece wants, and it is one of the better arguments for the four-minute celluloid as a musical proposition rather than just a commercial one.

records.title: I'm Sorry I Made You Cry
records.description:
N. J. Clesi's song of 1918 is a straightforward apology set to a slow waltz, and it was a substantial hit in the last year of the First World War — a period when American popular song swung between marching numbers and this sort of domestic regret. Henry Burr, by then the most recorded ballad singer in the country, was the natural voice for it.

The number matters here. A four-minute Indestructible at 3445 is a late record, made years after Columbia's distribution agreement had ended and after Edison's Blue Amberol had taken over the celluloid cylinder market. By 1918 Indestructible was the last independent cylinder maker of any size in the United States: Lambert had been driven out before 1907, the U-S Phonograph Company of Cleveland had gone under in 1913, and the whole rest of the industry had moved to discs.

Records from this final stretch are consequently less common than the Columbia-era ones, and they are the best evidence of how long the celluloid cylinder held on. The company kept going until 1922, when fire destroyed the Albany factory and ended American cylinder manufacture outside West Orange.

records.title: Good-Bye, Good Luck, God Bless You
records.description:
Ernest R. Ball wrote the music and J. Keirn Brennan the words, and the song belongs to the great wartime run of farewell ballads — the same vein as *Till We Meet Again* and *Keep the Home Fires Burning*, addressed by somebody staying behind to somebody leaving. Ball was among the most reliable songwriters of the period, and his ballads were recorded on every format then in production.

At 3572 this is one of the highest four-minute Indestructible numbers documented in this file, from the last years of the company. It is also one of the clearest illustrations of the label's late position: still recording the current hits, still selling a celluloid record, but doing so in a market where the cylinder had become a specialist product supported mainly by the people who already owned the machines.

Late Indestructibles like this one are worth handling carefully in spite of the brand name. The celluloid is durable, but the pasteboard core underneath is not, and a century of dry heat can shrink it enough that the cylinder no longer grips the mandrel — the commonest way a surviving Indestructible becomes unplayable.

records.title: The Holy City
records.description:
Stephen Adams's 1892 setting of Frederic Weatherly's *Holy City* was the most successful sacred ballad of its generation, and this is Indestructible's early two-minute reading of it by Henry Burr. The number is a low one, from the first years of the company's list, when the whole catalogue was still two-minute and the celluloid record was being sold as a novelty that could not be broken.

Fitting the song onto a two-minute cylinder means cutting it, and that is the interest of the record as against the later four-minute remake at 3364: the collector hears the compromise the format forced. Two minutes was enough for a verse and a chorus at speed, and no more.

Indestructible's earliest cylinders date from 1907, which puts a number in the 600s within the first year or so of production — before the Columbia distribution agreement, and while the company was still establishing that it could make and sell a moulded celluloid record at all in the face of Edison's patent claims.

records.title: Bonnie Doon
records.description:
"Ye banks and braes o' bonnie Doon" is Robert Burns, written in 1791 to an older Scots air, and it is one of the handful of Burns lyrics that became genuinely international parlour songs. The singer reproaches a landscape for being beautiful while he is not happy, which is a very Burns thing to do, and the tune is simple enough to survive any amount of Victorian arrangement.

Scottish and Irish songs were a staple of American cylinder catalogues out of all proportion to their place in the concert repertoire — they were familiar, they were out of copyright, and they suited the tenor voices the recording horn liked. Henry Burr, Canadian-born, sang a great many of them.

This is an early two-minute Indestructible, from the part of the list issued before the four-minute series began in 1909.

records.title: If You'll Remember Me
records.description:
A sentimental ballad from the early part of the Indestructible list, sung by Henry Burr. Its authorship has not been established here and no composer has been supplied; the title is common enough that guessing would be a poor service.

What can be said is where the record sits. A two-minute number in the 900s belongs to 1908 or thereabouts, which is the period in which the Columbia Phonograph Company gave up making its own cylinders and contracted to distribute Indestructible's instead. From that point until 1912 a buyer could take home the identical celluloid cylinder in a Columbia box, an Indestructible box, or — from Sears, Roebuck — an Oxford one.

For a collector that means the box, not the record, carries the brand. The cylinders themselves came out of the same moulds in Albany.

records.title: Daddy
records.description:
A late-Victorian parlour song of the kind that survived into the record era on sentiment alone, addressed by a child to a father. Its authorship has not been established here.

The record's interest is largely as a piece of the two-minute list. Indestructible kept its two-minute series alive right through the four-minute years and beyond — numbers in this range were still selling to owners of the enormous population of two-minute machines that had been bought between 1902 and 1908, and which no amount of four-minute advertising was going to make obsolete overnight.

Two-minute Indestructibles are, in general, more common today than the four-minute ones and less sought after; they are also the best cheap way to hear what the label's celluloid actually sounds like against contemporary black wax.

records.title: Abide With Me
records.description:
Henry Francis Lyte wrote the words in 1847 as he was dying; William Henry Monk's tune *Eventide* followed in 1861, and the two together produced one of the most widely sung hymns in English. It has been recorded continuously since the earliest days of the phonograph, and it remains the hymn most likely to turn up in an acoustic-era catalogue.

Hymns were serious commercial business for the cylinder companies. A machine sold on the strength of comic songs still had to have something to play on a Sunday, and every list carried a sacred section. Henry Burr, who recorded hundreds of them, was as much a gospel singer on record as a popular one.

The number places this in the two-minute series around 1909, at the point where Indestructible was also launching its four-minute records and the Columbia agreement was at its height.

records.title: I Want Somebody to Play With
records.description:
A light popular song of the late 1900s, recorded by Henry Burr for Indestructible's two-minute series. Neither its authorship nor its date of issue has been established here, and neither has been guessed at.

Records like this one are the ordinary fabric of a cylinder catalogue: songs bought from a publisher, recorded quickly, sold for a season and then dropped. They are also where the documentation for the independent labels fails soonest, because nobody thought them worth writing down. Edison's monthly supplements preserve that level of detail for the Edison catalogue; for Indestructible, the surviving evidence is mostly a number, a title and an artist in a collector's index.

That asymmetry is worth keeping in mind when comparing the two companies' catalogues. The Edison list looks better documented because it is, not because Edison issued a more coherent body of records.

records.title: Goodnight, Little Girl, Goodnight
records.description:
The two-minute version of a song Indestructible also issued at four minutes as 3052. Comparing the two, where a collector can find both, is one of the more instructive exercises available on this label: the same singer, the same song, cut to fit two different lengths a few years apart.

The two-minute cylinder turns at 160 grooves to the inch against the four-minute's 200, so the groove is wider and the stylus tracks it with less trouble — which is part of why two-minute records of any make tend to sound more robust than four-minute ones of the same vintage.

Henry Burr's ballads of this type are the substance of the Indestructible list. He had no exclusive contract with the Albany company, and the same voice singing the same repertoire can be found on Edison, Columbia and U-S Everlasting cylinders of the same years.

records.title: If I Had My Choice of the World's Pretty Girls
records.description:
A popular song of the late 1900s, sung by Henry Burr on Indestructible's two-minute series. Its authorship is not established here.

The long, faintly ridiculous title is characteristic of the period — publishers liked a title that told the whole joke, on the theory that a customer who could remember it could ask for it by name in a shop. The cylinder trade encouraged the habit, because a title printed on a box lid was the only advertising most records got.

The record belongs to the Columbia-distribution years, when Indestructible's two-minute cylinders had their widest circulation they would ever have. A copy found in a Columbia carton is not a different record; Columbia sold Albany's cylinders under its own name from 1908 until 1912.

records.title: Dinah Dear
records.description:
Arthur Collins was the leading baritone of the American record business in the 1900s and the voice of an enormous quantity of the minstrel-derived popular song of the period, alone and in partnership with Byron G. Harlan. *Dinah Dear* belongs to that repertoire, and modern listeners should expect the racial caricature that ran through it.

Collins recorded for every company that would pay him, which is why his name appears on Edison, Columbia, Victor, Indestructible and U-S Everlasting records of exactly the same years. The independent cylinder labels had no artist roster of their own in any meaningful sense; they hired the same freelancers out of the same New York studios.

The two-minute number places this in the Columbia-distribution period, when Indestructible cylinders were reaching more dealers than at any other time in the company's life.

records.title: I Wonder Who's Kissing Her Now
records.description:
Written for the 1909 Chicago musical *The Prince of Tonight* — music credited to Joseph E. Howard, with Harold Orlob's authorship established only decades later in court, and words by Will M. Hough and Frank R. Adams — this became one of the standard American popular songs of the century. Its question is a jealous one, and the tune's gentle waltz makes it sound anything but.

The song was a hit in exactly the season when Indestructible's cylinders were being distributed nationally by Columbia, and a two-minute number in the 1250s fits 1909 neatly. It would have reached buyers in Columbia and Indestructible boxes simultaneously.

Henry Burr's is one of a great many contemporary recordings; Edison issued the song on cylinder as well, so it is one of the titles where a direct comparison between wax and celluloid, on much the same repertoire and in the same year, is actually possible.

records.title: I'll Go Where You Want Me to Go
records.description:
A hymn of consecration — "I'll go where you want me to go, dear Lord" — from the late nineteenth century, and a fixture of the American revival repertoire. It is the sort of sacred song that sold steadily rather than spectacularly, and it stayed in cylinder catalogues for years at a time.

Henry Burr's gospel and hymn records are among the least discussed and most numerous of his output. He recorded the standard evangelical repertoire for practically every label, and the Indestructible sacred list leans on him heavily.

The two-minute number places this in the Columbia years. Sacred records in particular were kept in print far longer than popular songs, so a title like this may be found in boxes from more than one period of the company's life.

records.title: All Through the Night
records.description:
*Ar Hyd y Nos* is a Welsh air first printed in the eighteenth century, and its English lyric — "sleep my child and peace attend thee" — made it one of the best-loved lullabies in the language. Like most traditional material it cost the record companies nothing in royalties, which did no harm to its popularity in the catalogues.

Henry Burr's two-minute Indestructible is one of many acoustic-era recordings of the tune. Sung slowly, it is almost exactly two minutes long, which made it an unusually good fit for the short cylinder — one of the few songs of the period that did not have to be cut to fit.

The number belongs to the stretch of the two-minute list issued while Columbia was distributing Indestructible's records, which for a few years put these celluloid cylinders into shops in every part of the country.

records.description:
Herbert Ingraham's ballad of 1910, with words by Edgar Selden, was one of the better-selling sentimental songs of its year. Ingraham died young, in 1910, and this is among the songs his name is still attached to.

Henry Burr's Indestructible is a two-minute cylinder from the period after the four-minute series had begun, which is the significant thing about it. The Albany company did not treat the four-minute record as a replacement: it went on issuing new two-minute titles for years, because the machines in American parlours were overwhelmingly two-minute machines and would remain so for a long time.

That decision is one reason Indestructible outlived every other independent cylinder maker. It sold to the installed base rather than trying to convert it.

records.title: The Cubanola Glide
records.description:
Harry Von Tilzer's music and Vincent Bryan's words, published in 1909, gave the dance craze of that season its song — a "glide" with a mock-Cuban lilt, of a piece with the *Grizzly Bear* and the *Turkey Trot* that followed it. The number places the issue in the middle of the label's two-minute run. Von Tilzer songs turn up across all the cylinder catalogues of these years; the same title on an Edison cylinder is a straightforward comparison to make.

records.title: California and You
records.description:
A song of 1914 in the great American tradition of writing about a state you have not visited. It belongs to the boom in place-name songs that ran from *On the Banks of the Wabash* through to the 1920s, and it was current in the year war broke out in Europe.

Its authorship has not been confirmed here. What is documented is the pairing of the title with Henry Burr and with this two-minute Indestructible number, which places the record in the period after the Columbia agreement had ended — when Indestructible was selling under its own name and through the Sears Oxford brand, and was very nearly the only company in America still making new cylinders other than Edison.

Two-minute cylinders issued as late as this are a reminder of how long the short format survived. Edison had stopped making new two-minute wax records years earlier.

records.title: Good-Bye, Girls, I'm Through
records.description:
From *Chin-Chin*, the enormous 1914 Broadway spectacle built around the comedians Montgomery and Stone, with music by Ivan Caryll and lyrics by John Golden. The song is a bachelor's farewell to the field, and it was the show's most durable number.

Broadway material of this kind was recorded quickly and widely, and the cylinder companies took what they could get of it. Henry Burr's Indestructible is a two-minute record from the label's later years, when the company had outlived every American competitor except Edison and was working a much narrower market than it had in the Columbia days.

By 1914 the celluloid patent argument that had defined the company's first years was effectively over. Edison's own Blue Amberol had been on sale for two years, the U-S Phonograph Company had been litigated out of existence, and Indestructible simply carried on, quietly, until the Albany plant burned in 1922.

records.title: Ireland Must Be Heaven, for My Mother Came from There
records.description:
Fred Fisher's music with words by Joe McCarthy and Howard Johnson, published in 1916, is one of the best-known of the Irish-American mother songs — a genre that Tin Pan Alley worked hard for two decades and that sold enormously to an audience that was neither wholly Irish nor entirely sentimental about it.

The two-minute number places the record in the last third of the Indestructible list. By 1916 the cylinder was a minority format everywhere except in the homes that already had a machine, and the Albany company's business was largely with those homes.

records.title: Brighten the Corner Where You Are
records.description:
Ina Duley Ogdon's words and Charles H. Gabriel's tune, published in 1913, became the signature hymn of Billy Sunday's revival campaigns and one of the best-selling gospel songs of the decade. Its cheerfulness is aggressive, and it was meant to be sung by a very large number of people at once.

Records of the Sunday-campaign hymns sold in quantities that surprised the record companies, and every catalogue of the middle 1910s carries several. Henry Burr, who was as much a gospel recording artist as a popular one, sang most of them for somebody.

The two-minute Indestructible number places this among the label's late issues, from the years when the company was operating without Columbia's distribution and against a market that had largely moved to discs.

records.title: Hello Central, Give Me No Man's Land
records.description:
Irving Berlin wrote the music, Sam M. Lewis and Joe Young the words, and the song was published in 1918: a child telephones the operator asking to be connected to her father at the front. It is one of the most unashamedly manipulative songs of the war and it was among the biggest sellers of that year.

Henry Burr's two-minute Indestructible is one of the very latest records documented in this file. By 1918 Indestructible was the last independent cylinder manufacturer in the United States, still turning out celluloid records in Albany more than a decade after Edison's patent campaign had cleared the rest of the field.

Four years later a fire at the Albany plant ended it. The two-minute cylinder — a format Edison had stopped issuing new titles on around 1912 — outlived its inventor's interest in it by a decade, kept alive by the company he had spent years in court trying to stop.

records.title: In Darkest Africa
records.subtitle: from Sousa's Three Quotations
records.description:
Sousa's *Three Quotations* is a suite of three character pieces, and *In Darkest Africa* is the first of them — a piece of 1890s American band exotica whose title borrows Henry Morton Stanley's best-selling account of his Congo expedition. It is programme music of the sort every American band carried: a mood, some percussion colour, and a big finish.

This is one of the earliest Indestructible cylinders for which a release date is documented — June 1908, less than a year after the company began production, and just as the Columbia Phonograph Company was arranging to distribute its output. Band records were the backbone of the early list, partly because they recorded well and partly because they showed off what the celluloid surface could do with a loud ensemble.

The performing group is credited only as a band, and no name has been supplied here. Indestructible did not much bother identifying its studio ensembles, and the company's advertising put its emphasis elsewhere — on the record that could not be broken, could not wear out, and, in the phrase the company used, would last forever.
records.notes: Release date (June 1908), catalogue number and title come from the Mainspring Press streaming playlist of Indestructible cylinders, which gives discographical detail for each item. The performing group is credited only as 'Band' and none has been inferred. Indestructible's four-minute issues run in a 3000 series begun in 1909, separate from the two-minute list; a collector's listing of four-minute Indestructibles covering numbers in the 3020–3228 range is the direct evidence for that here. The box for this particular number was not examined. An Indestructible is a thin celluloid tube moulded over a pasteboard core with a metal ring pressed into each end. Those two bright rims are the fastest way to tell one from an Edison Blue Amberol, which is celluloid over a heavy plaster core and has no metal at the ends.

records.title: Bon Bon Buddy
records.description:
*Bon Bon Buddy* comes from *Bandanna Land*, the 1908 musical by the Black theatrical partnership of Bert Williams and George Walker, with music by Will Marion Cook and words by Alex Rogers. It was Walker's own song — "Bon Bon Buddy, the chocolate drop, that's me" — and it was the last great success of his career before illness ended it. That a song written and introduced by Black artists for a Black company on Broadway should have been recorded for the phonograph by white singers is entirely typical of the period and part of what makes the record worth studying.

Indestructible's two-minute version is credited to Billy Murray, the most successful American recording vocalist of the decade, whose diction and rhythmic snap made him the default choice for anything from the current shows. He recorded for everyone, and his presence on an independent cylinder label says nothing about exclusivity and everything about how the studios of 1908 worked.

The number places the record in the first full year of Indestructible production, at the moment the Columbia agreement was being made. It is early enough that a surviving copy may be found in either company's box.

records.title: I Remember You
records.description:
A two-minute Indestructible credited to Ada Jones, the English-born soprano who was the most popular female recording artist in America in the 1900s. Jones sang comic dialect songs, coy love songs and duets with Billy Murray and Len Spencer in enormous quantity, and she appears throughout the Indestructible list as she does in every other catalogue of the decade.

The identification of this record rests on a single digitised transfer whose Internet Archive identifier encodes the catalogue number. That is thinner evidence than most entries here and the number should be treated as unconfirmed; the transfer itself, however, can be heard, which is more than can be said for most of the label's list.

Jones's records are among the best reasons to seek out Indestructible cylinders specifically. Her voice sits in a range the acoustic horn handled well, and celluloid holds the sibilants of a comic lyric better than worn wax does.

records.title: Indian Intermezzo
records.description:
John J. Kimmel — born in Brooklyn to German parents, and billed on records under a dozen spellings of his name — was the most recorded accordionist of the acoustic era and the man who put Irish dance music onto American cylinders and discs in bulk. The "Indian intermezzo" was a fashion of the moment: a two-step with a tom-tom rhythm and a pentatonic tune, the same craze that produced *Hiawatha* and a hundred imitations.

This issue is documented as a June 1909 release, which puts it in the second year of the Columbia distribution agreement and the first year of the four-minute series. Solo instrumental records were good business for a cylinder company — a single loud instrument close to the horn was the easiest thing in the world to record well, and Kimmel's accordion is louder and cleaner on these cylinders than most contemporary singers.

Kimmel's Indestructibles are among the more sought-after items on the label, because his playing has an audience among traditional musicians that has nothing to do with phonograph collecting.

records.title: When You and I Were Young, Maggie
records.description:
The Columbia-branded issue of the Albany company's four-minute celluloid of Butterfield and Johnson's 1866 parlour standard, sung by the baritone Frank Coombs.

The arrangement behind this record is the most misunderstood thing about the independent cylinder trade. Columbia had been making cylinders since the 1890s, but by 1908 its business was in discs, and rather than keep a cylinder plant running it agreed to take Indestructible's celluloid records and sell them as its own. For four years, therefore, "Columbia Indestructible Records" were neither made nor recorded by Columbia. The moulds, the plant and the artists were Indestructible's; Columbia supplied the distribution and the name on the box.

For a collector the practical consequence is that a Columbia Indestructible and an Albany Indestructible of the same number are the same record. The value difference, where there is one, comes from the packaging and from which brand a given collection is organised around.

records.title: There's a Girl in Havana
records.description:
Helen Clark and Walter Van Brunt's duet on the 1911 stage song, in the four-minute celluloid form Columbia was selling under its own name in that year.

Columbia's decision to distribute rather than manufacture is a good measure of where the cylinder stood by 1908. The disc had won the mass market, and the cylinder had become a format for people who already owned a cylinder machine. Rather than invest in celluloid technology of its own — with Edison's patent lawyers waiting — Columbia took the cheaper route and sold somebody else's records.

Edison, meanwhile, was fighting the same technology in court and preparing to adopt it. The Blue Amberol of 1912 was Edison's own celluloid cylinder, and its arrival is what finally settled the argument the independents had started.

records.title: On Moonlight Bay
records.description:
The Clark and Van Brunt duet on Wenrich and Madden's 1912 hit, in the Columbia-branded form of the Albany four-minute celluloid.

By the end of 1912 Columbia had withdrawn, Indestructible was back to its own brand and to supplying Sears with Oxford-labelled copies, and Edison's Blue Amberol had put a celluloid cylinder into the hands of the man who had spent five years suing the people who made them.

records.title: I'd Love to Live in Loveland
records.description:
Henry Burr's four-minute reading of Will Rossiter's 1910 waltz song, in the form Columbia sold under its own name.

There is a nice irony in the Columbia Indestructible. Columbia and Edison had spent the 1890s and 1900s in more or less permanent litigation with each other, and here was Columbia putting its name on a record whose entire selling proposition — moulded celluloid that would not wear out — was the thing Edison was busy trying to suppress in the courts. Selling the independents' product was, among other things, a cheap way of keeping the pressure on.

For anyone sorting a shelf, the message is simple: the brand is on the box, the record is from Albany, and the number is the same either way.

John J. Kimmel's accordion solo, issued in June 1909 and sold in that period under both the Indestructible and Columbia names.

This is one of the few numbers in the file with a documented release month, which makes it a firm point inside the Columbia years — the agreement ran from 1908 to 1912, so a June 1909 issue is squarely within it. records.title: I Wonder Who's Kissing Her Now
records.description:
Henry Burr's two-minute celluloid of the 1909 hit from *The Prince of Tonight*, in the form Columbia put its own name on.

Columbia's cylinder customers in 1909 were buying, without necessarily knowing it, a record made by the company Edison was trying to litigate out of the celluloid business. That fight is the reason this catalogue has three names on it for one record. It is also the reason the American cylinder business ended up with exactly two survivors: Edison, who won the argument, and Indestructible, who outlasted it.

records.title: My Old Kentucky Home
records.description:
Stephen Foster published *My Old Kentucky Home, Good-Night!* in 1853, and by the 1900s it had become one of the fixed points of American song — sung, arranged and recorded continuously, and adopted as the state song of Kentucky in 1928. Quartet arrangements of the Foster songs were a staple of every record catalogue, and the Peerless Quartette sang more of them than most.

The U-S Phonograph Company of Cleveland, Ohio, put its U-S Everlasting celluloid cylinders on the market in 1909, entering the same argument Indestructible was already in the middle of: whether anyone other than Edison could make a moulded celluloid record. Edison's patent suits followed, and the company was gone by 1913 — the shortest-lived of the significant American cylinder makers, and the clearest single casualty of the celluloid litigation.

That short life is why U-S Everlastings are scarcer than Indestructibles today, and why the surviving numerical documentation for the label is thinner still. Duane Deakins's index of the label, compiled decades later from collectors' shelves, remains the main published guide to what was issued.

records.title: The Whistling Bowery Boy
records.description:
The Lambert Company of Chicago is where the celluloid cylinder begins. Thomas B. Lambert patented a process for moulding records in celluloid at the turn of the century and began selling them around 1900 — pink, black and white tubes, unbreakable, and unaffected by the mould and shrinkage that plagued wax. They were years ahead of anything else on the market.

They were also, from Edison's point of view, an infringement. The litigation that followed ran for years and was ruinous for a company of Lambert's size; the firm left the record business around 1906, and the celluloid cylinder passed to the Indestructible Record Company of Albany, which began production in 1907. Every celluloid cylinder that followed — Indestructible, U-S Everlasting, Oxford, and eventually Edison's own Blue Amberol — descends from what Lambert started.

This particular record, a whistling solo dated 1903, is a good example of the popular repertoire on the label. The whistler is not identified in the documentation seen here, and none has been guessed at. Lambert cylinders are genuinely rare today: production was small, the company was short-lived, and although the celluloid itself survives well, the market for them was over before most collectors were born.
